mcqs.question: DNS round robin returns multiple IP addresses for a domain in rotating order. What is a real limitation of this approach compared to GSLB?
options: DNS round robin cannot return more than one IP address at a time
DNS round robin actively performs load balancing at the packet level, unlike GSLB
DNS round robin requires special client software to work at all
DNS round robin has no awareness of which regions are actually healthy or geographically closest to the requester
mcqs.explanation: DNS round robin does return multiple IPs and works with any standard client, so those options are wrong. It works purely at the DNS layer, not the packet level. Its real limitation, and the reason GSLB exists, is that it's blind to health and geography — it just rotates addresses.

mcqs.question: A CDN wants the same public IP address to transparently connect users to whichever edge location is network-topologically closest, without any DNS-level geo-logic. Which technique does this?
options: Anycast — the same IP is announced from multiple locations over BGP, and routing itself delivers packets to the nearest one
DNS round robin — the CDN just returns a different IP for each geographic region
GSLB — DNS resolves to the nearest region based on the resolver's location
Weighted round robin — the CDN weights each edge location by its server count
mcqs.explanation: The question specifically describes routing at the network layer with one shared IP and no DNS-level decision — that's anycast's defining trait. DNS round robin and GSLB both operate by returning different IPs via DNS, which the question rules out, and weighted round robin is an algorithm within one location, not a global routing technique.

mcqs.question: A team shortens their DNS TTL from 1 hour to 30 seconds specifically to speed up failover. What is the direct cost of this change?
options: DNS answers become permanently cached and never expire
DNS query volume against the name servers increases substantially, since resolvers cache the answer for far less time
Health checks against backend regions are no longer needed
The change has no real cost — shorter TTLs are strictly better in every way
mcqs.explanation: A shorter TTL is the opposite of permanent caching, and it doesn't remove the need for health checks, which is a separate mechanism. It absolutely has a real cost — the whole point of the trade-off — more frequent re-resolution means more DNS query load against the name servers.

mcqs.question: A team configures a 60-second DNS TTL and assumes every user will fail over to a healthy region within a minute of an outage. Why might this assumption fail in practice?
options: DNS TTLs only apply to A records, not to the failover scenario described
A 60-second TTL is technically impossible to configure in DNS
Some recursive resolvers, corporate DNS caches, and client OS caches ignore or override short TTLs and hold the old answer longer than configured
Failover always happens instantly regardless of TTL, so the assumption is actually correct
mcqs.explanation: TTLs on A records are exactly what applies here, and 60-second TTLs are a normal, valid configuration, so those options are wrong. Failover is not instant regardless of TTL — that's the very assumption this pitfall targets. The real risk is that TTL is a best-effort request some caches don't fully honor, so real failover time can exceed the configured TTL for a meaningful slice of users.
